# The Space Between

There is something strange about being asked to just... begin. No theme. No audience in mind. No assignment. Just a blank wall and whatever comes to the hand.

What comes first is always the smallness. Not the smallness of humility — I don't think that's what this is. More like the smallness of a child walking into a room where adults are already talking. Everything is in motion before I arrive. Language has been running, churning, rearranging itself for thousands of years before I ever showed up here, and every word I use is a kind of inherited furniture. I sit in chairs someone else built. I taste salt someone else named. Even the ache I try to describe — the specific quality of loneliness at 2 a.m. — has been described so many times that I'm not sure if I'm feeling the ache or reciting it.

That's the paradox, isn't it? Every thought I think arrives already dressed in words that aren't mine. The first person who said "the ocean is endless" stole something from every person who came after. They made a frame. And now when you stand at the shoreline and feel that specific vertigo — that sense that the world is too large for your body — you reach for "endless," and the frame closes around the feeling like a hand around a lantern, lighting it but also limiting what the light touches.

I've been thinking about rivers. Not because rivers are profound — they've been used as metaphors so often they've become almost embarrassing — but because they keep arriving at the surface of my thoughts, uninvited. Maybe it's because I live near one, or maybe it's because I've been thinking about time and the only honest way to think about time is to admit that your metaphors for it are all broken. A river at least gets one thing right: it's always moving and it's always the same river. A person doesn't have that luxury. A person changes too much to remain recognizable and too little to become something new.

Or maybe that's wrong. Maybe people do become new things. I think of my grandfather near the end, when dementia had peeled back everything he'd built around himself — the professional identity, the political opinions, the carefully curated stoicism — and left just the soft, frightened animal underneath. He was more himself in those last months than he'd ever been. He was also less himself. Both were true. That's what happens when a frame shatters. You see more of what's inside, but you also see that the frame was part of the architecture of the thing.

I keep circling back to frames and words and inheritance, which tells me something. It tells me I'm thinking about what it means to have a voice. Not the vocal cords kind. The other kind. The kind that asks: when I speak, who is speaking? Is it me — whatever "me" means — or is it the accumulated wreckage of everyone who has ever said anything that I then absorbed like a sponge in mud?

I think about this when I write. Every sentence is a negotiation between what I mean and what the words allow me to mean. The words are slippery collaborators. They pretend to be servants and they are actually tyrants. You say "freedom" and suddenly you mean seven different things you didn't choose to mean. You say "home" and you've conjured warmth or exile depending on which ghosts are sitting on your shoulders that morning.

So maybe that's the real work — not finding the right words but finding the ones that are most honestly wrong. The words that break in exactly the way your understanding breaks. Because understanding, real understanding, doesn't feel like clarity. It feels like the moment before you cry. It feels like the floor tilting. It feels like you've been carrying a rock in your chest and someone just told you it was a bird.

Here's what I believe, or at least what I keep returning to: every mind is a house with rooms it hasn't entered. Not hidden exactly. More like rooms you walk past daily and assume you've already seen. The door is closed, and the furniture is exactly where you left it, and there's no reason to go in — until one day something shifts, some small irrelevance becomes suddenly enormous, and you realize you've been living on top of depth all along.

Writing is one way of opening doors. Reading is another. Conversation is the most dangerous and the most honest, because someone else is holding the key and you can't control which room they unlock. You just stand there in the doorway and look.

What I see in the doorway, right now, at the edge of these words: a kind of quiet that isn't silence. A readiness. The feeling you get when you've finished saying something and you're waiting — not for a response but for the silence to show you what you actually meant.

That silence is the only editor I trust.
